assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED opened a new regime of light-matter interaction on a chip: strong coupling of a superconducting artificial atom to a single microwave photon, giving dispersive readout, photon-mediated qubit coupling and the architecture used in essentially all superconducting quantum processors. It is a clean, controllable demonstration of basic quantum optics in a solid-state circuit, which is exactly the type of discovery the prize rewards, and it has been reproduced across many laboratories.
assessment.attribution: Blais with Huang, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 proposal and Wallraff with Schoelkopf and co-workers made the 2004 Nature strong-coupling experiment, so theory plus experiment give a natural trio. Girvin and Huang are not in the supplied credited names, and Devoret's circuit work overlaps and was already honoured, so the allocation is not entirely clean.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature: more than twenty years of independent confirmation and a robust interpretation. Timing is delicate because the 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits; a prompt follow-on for cQED can be defended as a distinct discovery, but some colleagues may prefer to wait.
uncertainties: Close overlap with the 2025 prize and the committee may judge it too soon after.
Allocation of credit among Blais, Girvin, Huang, Schoelkopf and Wallraff is not settled by the supplied names.
My own field and close collaborations in this community create potential conflict of interest, so I may be biased in its favour; this is flagged for the committee.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal and its experimental realisation with trapped ions established a fully controllable quantum-computing and simulation platform with the highest gate fidelities and longest coherence of any platform. The physics is clear and fundamental: laser control of individual quantum systems.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive 1995 proposal; Blatt led the experimental realisation of gates, entanglement and algorithms. Wineland (2012 prize) and others such as Monroe and Wineland's NIST group contributed to the experimental development, which could complicate fair allocation. The supplied trio is coherent.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed by many groups. The 2012 prize to Wineland and Haroche partly covers the control of single ions, so the novelty relative to that prize must be argued.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize for ion control.
Role of Monroe and the NIST group is not in the supplied credit.
Scalability to fault-tolerant machines remains unproven, though the prize rewards the discovery rather than the application.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution turned the foundations of quantum mechanics into a concept of information security with a concrete protocol (BB84) and an entanglement-based variant (E91). It has had lasting conceptual impact on quantum information and led to field and satellite demonstrations.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard are the clear originators of BB84, and Ekert of the entanglement-based protocol; Pan led the main experimental and networking advances but a three-person limit forces a choice of the theory trio. Weighing protocol invention against experimental realisation is not straightforward, and Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is not among the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: The protocols are decades old and the interpretation is stable, but real-world security rests on implementations and practical attacks; networks are still developing. The 2022 prize on entanglement and Bell tests partly covers the foundations.
uncertainties: Whether implementation security is mature enough to reward the application side.
Choice between theory trio and including Pan.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock with magic-wavelength trapping, proposed by Katori and brought to extraordinary accuracy and stability by Ye's group, is a clean precision-measurement result with consequences for metrology, tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. The control of many atoms in a lattice at the 10^-18 level is an impressive demonstration of quantum control.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the magic-wavelength proposal and early demonstration; Ye's group drove the accuracy and many-body clock work. A two-person prize is feasible, though Hall, Hansch and Wineland-type clock contributions were already rewarded earlier.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, with confirmation by many national labs and routine comparisons across laboratories. A redefinition of the second is pending and could reinforce timing.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier prizes for frequency combs and ion clocks.
Ye also appears in other candidates, which could affect combinatorial choices of laureates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, from the superfluid-Mott transition to quantum gas microscopes, gave a controllable platform to realise Hubbard models and study strongly correlated dynamics. It is a clear case of an engineered quantum system opening a new regime.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch proposed the Hubbard-model realisation, Greiner and Bloch performed the pioneering experiments and microscopes. Cirac and Hänsch's group and others also contributed, so several people are plausible; Bloch, Greiner and Zoller seems the cleanest trio.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely replicated. The BEC prize of 2001 and the broader cold-atom prizes overlap partially, so the specific new contribution must be defined.
uncertainties: Quantification of how many unsolved problems have been solved by quantum simulators remains debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction made fault-tolerant quantum computing conceivable by showing that errors can be suppressed with redundancy. Shor's code, Steane's code and Kitaev's surface-code ideas have profoundly shaped the field and experimental programmes.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane produced the first codes and Kitaev the topological codes and fault-tolerance concept; Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme and others also contributed, so credit is diffuse.
assessment.maturity: The theory is solid, and recent below-threshold experiments on superconducting and ion devices are encouraging, but full-scale error correction has not been demonstrated. This is theory whose experimental confirmation is still developing, so recognition may be premature.
uncertainties: Whether experiments are mature enough, as I note that full-scale error correction is still ahead.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling mechanical oscillators to their quantum ground state and controlling them with light and microwaves opened a regime where macroscopic objects display quantum behaviour. It links closely to the physics honoured in 2025 and has applications to quantum transduction and sensing.
assessment.attribution: Teufel, Cleland, Painter, Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer all made decisive demonstrations, five names are credited and a maximum of three can be chosen, so any selection leaves out major contributors, which is a real difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by several independent groups on different platforms, with stable interpretation, but the field is still evolving.
uncertainties: Five or more equally deserving contributors for three places.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays with optical tweezers provide a flexible platform for quantum simulation and computing, with demonstrations of new quantum phases and growing gate fidelities. This is important and rapidly developing.
assessment.attribution: Browaeys and Lukin led early array experiments and Saffman contributed gate proposals; Zoller's theoretical role (also in other candidates) is central. A fair trio is possible but contested.
assessment.maturity: Strong recent progress, confirmed by multiple groups, though the field is young, so recognition may be premature relative to the other atomic candidates.
uncertainties: Timeliness as the field is still developing.
Contested allocation with Zoller and others.
